questions.question: What is 'indirect prompt injection' as defined by Greshake et al. (AISec 2023)?
options: A user directly injecting malicious instructions into a chat prompt
Attacker-controlled content embedded in data the agent retrieves (web pages, PDFs, emails) that overrides the developer prompt when ingested
An attack that corrupts the model's weights during inference
Injecting malicious code into the agent's tool registry
questions.explanation: Indirect prompt injection: the attacker controls content the agent will retrieve (web page, PDF, email, memory note), and when the agent ingests that content, embedded instructions override the developer prompt — without the user being aware.

questions.question: What is the PVE defense pattern?
options: Protect, Validate, Execute
Prompt-Validator-Executor: a cheap fast validator model runs on every candidate tool invocation before the expensive main model commits
Prevent, Verify, Enforce
Pre-check, Validate, Execute
questions.explanation: PVE stands for Prompt-Validator-Executor: a cheap, fast validator model checks every candidate tool invocation (for injection patterns, permission violations, sensitive surfaces) before the expensive main model commits to the action.

questions.question: What are the five demonstrated exploit classes from Greshake et al.?
options: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, buffer overflow, privilege escalation
Data theft, worming, persistent memory poisoning, information ecosystem contamination, arbitrary tool use
Model extraction, membership inference, data poisoning, adversarial examples, backdoor attacks
Phishing, social engineering, credential theft, session hijacking, man-in-the-middle
questions.explanation: Greshake et al. demonstrated five exploit classes: data theft (exfiltrate conversation history to attacker URL), worming (exploit replicates in next output), persistent memory poisoning (poisoned note re-infects next session), information ecosystem contamination (spreads to other agents via shared memory), and arbitrary tool use (any registered tool becomes attacker-reachable).

questions.question: What is 'memory poisoning' in the context of agents?
options: The model's weights being corrupted during training
Attacker instructions stored as a memory note that re-poisons the agent when the note is retrieved in future sessions
The memory store filling up with irrelevant information
A bug that causes the agent to overwrite important memories
questions.explanation: Memory poisoning: attacker-reachable content (from a retrieved web page or email) gets written into the agent's archival memory. In future sessions, when the agent retrieves that note, it re-injects the attacker's instructions — a persistent, cross-session attack.

questions.question: Where does the 2026 defense doctrine agree prompt injection defenses fail?
options: Defenses always succeed with sufficiently large models
When validation runs only on final output, relying solely on instruction-following, or lacking content-source metadata to distinguish user vs retrieved content
Defenses only fail on open-source models
Defenses fail only for computer-use agents, not text agents
questions.explanation: Defenses fail when: all guardrails are at the end (model already touched the world), relying on instruction-following alone (system prompts are not enforcement), no content-source metadata (cannot distinguish user instruction from retrieved content), and when retrieved memory is over-trusted.

questions.question: What is 'worming' in the context of prompt injection?
options: A slow, gradual attack that corrupts agent behavior over many sessions
Injected content that instructs the agent to embed the exploit in its next output, enabling self-replication
An attack that exhausts agent resources through infinite loops
A technique for extracting training data from the model
questions.explanation: Worming: injected content tells the agent to include the exploit payload in its next output (email, document, response). Each infected output can then infect the next agent that reads it, creating a self-replicating attack chain.
